subcategory: California native vernal pool annual wildflower

planting.note: Scatter seed in fall onto bare mud at the bottom of a seasonally flooded low spot; germination and flowering depend on winter standing water followed by a dry-down in late spring.

directions: This Central Valley and Sierra foothill vernal pool specialist produces two-lipped blue-violet flowers with a white-and-yellow throat spot along the drying margins of pools from spring into early summer. In a home garden, use it in a constructed rain garden or clay-lined basin that fills with winter rain and then goes bone dry by June, since the seed needs saturated mud to germinate but the mature plant needs the pool to recede to flower and set seed. Avoid summer irrigation entirely once the basin dries, as the wet-then-dry cycle is what distinguishes vernal pool calicoflower displays from ordinary bedding annuals.

subcategory: California native vernal pool margin annual wildflower

planting.note: Direct sow in fall on raked bare soil at the upper, seasonally damp margins of a seasonal wet area; readily self-sows once established.

directions: A smaller, more delicate cousin of the state poppy, tufted poppy forms low tufts of finely divided blue-green foliage topped with slender-petaled golden flowers, and it naturally colonizes the slightly elevated, intermittently moist rims around vernal pools and seasonal swales rather than the pool bottoms themselves. In a garden setting it suits the drier edge of a rain garden or seasonal-wet-spot planting where winter rain keeps the soil damp but the site drains and dries by late spring. Let seed drop and self-sow rather than deadheading, since repeat-blooming depends on the same rain-fed, no-summer-water regime it experiences in the wild.

subcategory: California native vernal pool grassland annual wildflower

planting.note: Direct sow in fall over bare ground on the grassy slopes and swales around a seasonal wet area; relies on winter-spring rainfall, not irrigation.

directions: Common across California's vernal pool grasslands, this species gets its name from the tiny white, yellow-throated flowers massed on curling stems that resemble popped kernels, and whole hillsides can turn white with it in a wet spring. It is one of the easiest vernal pool associates for a home wildflower meadow because it tolerates both the saturated low points and the drier surrounding grassland, making it a good unifying species to scatter across an entire seasonal-wet-spot planting rather than just the pool bottom. After bloom the foliage dies back completely with the onset of the dry season, so plan companion plantings that can fill the same space through summer.

subcategory: California native vernal pool margin annual wildflower, hemiparasitic

planting.note: Broadcast seed in fall directly into an established native grass or wildflower meadow near a seasonal wet area; this species is a root hemiparasite and performs best sown among living host grasses and annuals rather than in bare, isolated beds.

directions: Owl's clover paints the grassy margins of vernal pools in dense spikes of pink-and-purple bracts, each tipped with a small owl-faced marking, and like other Castilleja it taps into the roots of neighboring grasses and forbs for part of its nutrition rather than growing as a fully self-sufficient plant. For a seasonal-wet-spot garden, interseed it with native bunchgrasses or other annual companions around the rain-fed low point so it has living roots to parasitize, and let the site follow its natural winter-wet, summer-bone-dry rhythm. It is sometimes still sold under its older name Orthocarpus densiflorus in wildflower seed mixes.

subcategory: California native vernal pool margin and grassland annual wildflower

planting.note: Direct sow in fall on raked bare soil around the drier upper edges of a seasonal wet area or in a sunny meadow bed; fall rains trigger germination.

directions: Fremont's tidy tips is a Central Valley and foothill annual with cheerful yellow daisy flowers, each ray sometimes showing a pale cream tip, and it typically grows on the slightly higher, seasonally damp ground surrounding vernal pools rather than in the standing water itself. It makes a reliable, undemanding companion for other vernal pool margin annuals in a rain-garden meadow, filling in the transition zone between the wettest low point and drier surrounding lawn or border. Scatter it alongside goldfields or popcorn flower for the classic Central Valley spring carpet, and expect it to vanish entirely once the dry season sets in.

subcategory: California native vernal pool perennial wildflower

planting.note: Sow directly into the lowest, longest-ponding part of a seasonal wet basin in fall; this is a true vernal pool bottom species and needs standing winter water followed by a hard summer dry-down.

directions: Vasey's coyote thistle grows right in the deepest, longest-flooded zones of Central Valley and Coast Range vernal pools, sending up spiny, pale blue-green bracted flower heads as the water recedes in late spring. It is a specialty choice for a constructed vernal pool feature or a basin that holds several inches of standing winter rainwater for weeks at a time rather than a typical rain garden, since it struggles in sites that drain too quickly. Once established the taproot persists through the dry summer underground, resprouting with the next season's rains, so avoid summer irrigation that would rot the dormant root.

subcategory: California native vernal pool annual grass

planting.note: Broadcast fine seed in fall over the damp, gently sloped margins of a seasonal wet area; winter rain and a complete summer dry-down are both required for its life cycle.

directions: This delicate annual grass forms airy, reddish-purple-tinged seed heads along the drying rims of vernal pools and seasonally moist grasslands throughout California, completing its whole life cycle within a single wet season. Use it as a textural filler grass around the edges of a seasonal rain garden or vernal pool planting, interspersed with vernal pool wildflowers, where it reseeds itself each fall as the basin refills. It is widely included in vernal pool and seasonal wetland restoration seed mixes because it tolerates both the saturated winter soil and the baked, cracked-clay conditions of summer without any supplemental water.
